entries.7c5ed0d17369bab57b1ad8917fa4b806cfbb93af: <div sID="gen33509" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="1Pet.5" sID="1Pet.5"/> <div eID="gen33509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33510" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33511" type="x-p"/> In which the apostle gives particular directions, first to the elders, how to behave themselves towards their flock (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.1-1Pet.5.4">ver. 1-4</reference>); then to the younger, to be obedient and humble, and to cast their care upon God, <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.5-1Pet.5.7">ver. 5-7</reference>. He then exhorts all to sobriety, watchfulness against temptations, and stedfastness in the faith, praying earnestly for them; and so concludes his epistle with a solemn doxology, mutual salutations, and his apostolical benediction.
entries.23ab8653fd3bed2faf64f02fcef898a9589a2a66: <div eID="gen33511" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33510" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Advice to Elders. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen33512" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The elders which are among you I exhort, who am also an elder, and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and also a partaker of the glory that shall be revealed: <hi type="super">2</hi> Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight <hi type="italic">thereof,</hi> not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind; <hi type="super">3</hi> Neither as being lords over <hi type="italic">God's</hi> heritage, but being ensamples to the flock. <hi type="super">4</hi> And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away. <div eID="gen33512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33513" type="x-p"/> Here we may observe, <div eID="gen33513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33514" type="x-p"/> I. The persons to whom this exhortation is given—to the presbyters, pastors, and spiritual guides of the church, elders by office, rather than by age, ministers of those churches to whom he wrote this epistle. <div eID="gen33514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33515" type="x-p"/> II. The person who gives this exhortation—the apostle Peter: <hi type="italic">I exhort;</hi> and, to give force to this exhortation, he tells them he was their brother-presbyter or fellow-elder, and so puts nothing upon them but what he was ready to perform himself. He was also <hi type="italic">a witness of the sufferings of Christ,</hi> being with him in the garden, attending him to the palace of the high-priest, and very likely being a spectator of his suffering upon the cross, at a distance among the crowd, <reference osisRef="Acts.3.15">Acts iii. 15</reference>. He adds that he was also <hi type="italic">a partaker of the glory</hi> that was in some degree revealed at the transfiguration (<reference osisRef="Matt.17.1-Matt.17.3">Matt. xvii. 1-3</reference>), and shall be completely enjoyed at the second coming of Jesus Christ. Learn, 1. Those whose office it is to teach others ought carefully to study their own duty, as well as teach the people theirs. 2. How different the spirit and behaviour of Peter were from that of his pretended successors! He does not command and domineer, but exhort. He does not claim sovereignty over all pastors and churches, nor style himself <hi type="italic">prince of the apostles, vicar of Christ,</hi> or <hi type="italic">head of the church,</hi> but values himself upon being an <hi type="italic">elder.</hi> All the apostles were elders, though every elder was not an apostle. 3. It was the peculiar honour of Peter, and a few more, to be the witnesses of Christ's sufferings; but it is the privilege of all true Christians to be partakers of the glory that shall be revealed. <div eID="gen33515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33516" type="x-p"/> III. The pastor's duty described, and the manner in which that duty ought to be performed. The pastoral duty is three-fold:—1. <hi type="italic">To feed the flock,</hi> by preaching to them the sincere word of God, and ruling them according to such directions and discipline as the word of God prescribes, both which are implied in this expression, <hi type="italic">Feed the flock.</hi> 2. The pastors of the church must <hi type="italic">take the oversight thereof.</hi> The elders are exhorted to do the office of bishops (as the word signifies), by personal care and vigilance over all the flock committed to their charge. 3. They must be <hi type="italic">examples to the flock,</hi> and practise the holiness, self-denial, mortification, and all other Christian duties, which they preach and recommend to their people. These duties must be performed, <hi type="italic">not by constraint,</hi> not because you must do them, not from compulsion of the civil power, or the constraint of fear or shame, but from a willing mind that takes pleasure in the work: <hi type="italic">not for filthy lucre,</hi> or any emoluments and profits attending the place where you reside, or any perquisite belonging to the office, <hi type="italic">but of a ready mind,</hi> regarding the flock more than the fleece, sincerely and cheerfully endeavouring to serve the church of God; <hi type="italic">neither as being lords over God's heritage,</hi> tyrannizing over them by compulsion and coercive force, or imposing unscriptural and human inventions upon them instead of necessary duty, <reference osisRef="Matt.20.25-Matt.20.26">Matt. xx. 25, 26</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.24">2 Cor. i. 24</reference>. Learn, (1.) The eminent dignity of the church of God, and all the true members of it. These poor, dispersed, suffering Christians were the flock of God. The rest of the world is a brutal herd. These are an orderly flock, redeemed to God by the great Shepherd, living in holy love and communion one with another, <hi type="italic">according to the will of God.</hi> They are also dignified with the title of God's <hi type="italic">heritage</hi> or <hi type="italic">clergy,</hi> his peculiar lot, chosen out of the common multitude for his own people, to enjoy his special favour and to do him special service. The word is never restricted in the New Testament to the ministers of religion. (2.) The pastors of the church ought to consider their people as <hi type="italic">the flock of God, as God's heritage,</hi> and treat them accordingly. They are not theirs, to be lorded over at pleasure; but they are God's people, and should be treated with love, meekness, and tenderness, for the sake of him to whom they belong. (3.) Those ministers who are either driven to the work by necessity or drawn to it by filthy lucre can never perform their duty as they ought, because they do not do it willingly, and with a ready mind. (4.) The best way a minister can take to engage the respect of a people is to discharge his own duty among them in the best manner that he can, and to be a constant example to them of all that is good. <div eID="gen33516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33517" type="x-p"/> IV. In opposition to that filthy lucre which many propose to themselves as their principal motive in undertaking and discharging the pastoral office, the apostle sets before them the crown of glory designed by the great shepherd, Jesus Christ, for all his faithful ministers. Learn, 1. Jesus Christ is <hi type="italic">the chief shepherd</hi> of the whole flock and heritage of God. He bought them, and rules them; he defends and saves them for ever. He is also the chief shepherd over all inferior shepherds; they derive their authority from him, act in his name, and are accountable to him at last. 2. This chief shepherd will appear, to judge all ministers and under-shepherds, to call them to account, whether they have faithfully discharged their duty both publicly and privately according to the foregoing directions. 3. Those that are found to have done their duty shall have what is infinitely better than temporal gain; they shall receive from the grand shepherd a high degree of everlasting glory, <hi type="italic">a crown of glory that fadeth not away.</hi>
entries.d371aa99d6cb97aeb206163ae882b1d07bdfbc72: <div eID="gen33517" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Humility Recommended. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen33518" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Likewise, ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder. Yea, all <hi type="italic">of you</hi> be subject one to another, and be clothed with humility: for God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble. <hi type="super">6</hi> Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time: <hi type="super">7</hi> Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you. <div eID="gen33518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33519" type="x-p"/> Having settled and explained the duty of the pastors or spiritual guides of the church, the apostle comes now to instruct the flock, <div eID="gen33519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33520" type="x-p"/> I. How to behave themselves to their ministers and to one another. He calls them <hi type="italic">the younger,</hi> as being generally younger than their grave pastors, and to put them in mind of their inferiority, the term younger being used by our Saviour to signify an inferior, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.26">Luke xxii. 26</reference>. He exhorts those that are younger and inferior to <hi type="italic">submit themselves to the elder,</hi> to give due respect and reverence to their persons, and to yield to their admonitions, reproof, and authority, enjoining and commanding what the word of God requires, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.17">Heb. xiii. 17</reference>. As to one another, the rule is that they should all <hi type="italic">be subject one to another,</hi> so far as to receive the reproofs and counsels one of another, and be ready to <hi type="italic">bear one another's burdens,</hi> and perform all the offices of friendship and charity one to another; and particular persons should submit to the directions of the whole society, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.21">Eph. v. 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.16">Jam. v. 16</reference>. These duties of submission to superiors in age or office, and subjection to one another, being contrary to the proud nature and selfish interests of men, he advises them to <hi type="italic">be clothed with humility.</hi> "Let your minds, behaviour, garb, and whole frame, be adorned with humility, as the most beautiful habit you can wear; this will render obedience and duty easy and pleasant; but, if you be disobedient and proud, God will set himself to oppose and crush you; for <hi type="italic">he resisteth the proud,</hi> when he <hi type="italic">giveth grace to the humble.</hi>" Observe, 1. Humility is the great preserver of peace and order in all Christian churches and societies, consequently pride is the great disturber of them, and the cause of most dissensions and breaches in the church. 2. There is a mutual opposition between God and the proud, so the word signifies; they war against him, and he scorns them; <hi type="italic">he resisteth the proud,</hi> because they are like the devil, enemies to himself and to his kingdom among men, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.34">Prov. iii. 34</reference>. 3. Where God giveth grace to be humble, he will give more grace, more wisdom, faith, holiness, and humility. Hence the apostle adds: <hi type="italic">Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.6">v. 6</reference>. "Since God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace to the humble, therefore humble yourselves, not only one to another, but to the great God, whose judgments are coming upon the world, and must begin at the house of God (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17">ch. iv. 17</reference>); his hand is almighty, and can easily pull you down if you be proud, or exalt you if you be humble; and it will certainly do it, either in this life, if he sees it best for you, or at the day of general retribution." Learn, (1.) The consideration of the omnipotent hand of God should make us humble and submissive to him in all that he brings upon us. (2.) Humbling ourselves to God under his hand is the next way to deliverance and exaltation; patience under his chastisements, and submission to his pleasure, repentance, prayer, and hope in his mercy, will engage his help and release in due time, <reference osisRef="Jas.4.7">Jam. iv. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jas.4.10">10</reference>. <div eID="gen33520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33521" type="x-p"/> II. The apostle, knowing that these Christians were already under very hard circumstances, rightly supposes that what he had foretold of greater hardships yet a coming might excite in them abundance of care and fear about the event of these difficulties, what the issue of them would be to themselves, their families, and the church of God; foreseeing this anxious care would be a heavy burden, and a sore temptation, he gives them the best advice, and supports it with a strong argument. His advice is to <hi type="italic">cast all their care,</hi> or <hi type="italic">all care of themselves, upon God.</hi> "Throw your cares, which are so cutting and distracting, which wound your souls and pierce your hearts, upon the wise and gracious providence of God; trust in him with a firm composed mind, <hi type="italic">for he careth for you.</hi> He is willing to release you of your care, and take the care of you upon himself. He will either avert what you fear, or support you under it. He will order all events to you so as shall convince you of his paternal love and tenderness towards you; and all shall be so ordered that no hurt, but good, shall come unto you," <reference osisRef="Matt.6.25">Matt. vi. 25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.84.11">Ps. lxxxiv. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.28">Rom. viii. 28</reference>. Learn, 1. The best of Christians are apt to labour under the burden of anxious and excessive care; the apostle calls it, <hi type="italic">all your care,</hi> intimating that the cares of Christians are various and of more sorts than one: personal cares, family cares, cares for the present, cares for the future, cares for themselves, for others, and for the church. 2. The cares even of good people are very burdensome, and too often very sinful; when they arise from unbelief and diffidence, when they torture and distract the mind, unfit us for the duties of our place and hinder our delightful service of God, they are very criminal. 3. The best remedy against immoderate care is to <hi type="italic">cast our care upon God,</hi> and resign every event to the wise and gracious determination. A firm belief of the rectitude of the divine will and counsels calms the spirit of man. <hi type="italic">We ceased, saying, The will of the Lord be done,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.21.14">Acts xxi. 14</reference>.
entries.caa02c4c3865fa2972dcd5281db7f6f2db06c7e9: <div eID="gen33521" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Sobriety and Vigilance Enjoined. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen33522" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour: <hi type="super">9</hi> Whom resist stedfast in the faith, knowing that the same afflictions are accomplished in your brethren that are in the world. <div eID="gen33522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33523" type="x-p"/> Here the apostle does three things:— <div eID="gen33523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33524" type="x-p"/> I. He shows them their danger from an enemy more cruel and restless than even the worst of men, whom he describes, <div eID="gen33524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33525" type="x-p"/> 1. By his characters and names. (1.) He is an adversary: "<hi type="italic">That adversary of yours;</hi> not a common adversary, but an enemy that impleads you, and litigates against you in your grand depending cause, and aims at your very souls." (2.) <hi type="italic">The devil, the grand accuser of all the brethren;</hi> this title is derived from a word which signifies to strike through, or to stab. He would strike malignity into our natures and poison into our souls. If he could have struck these people with passion and murmuring in their sufferings, perhaps he might have drawn them to apostasy and ruin. (3.) He is <hi type="italic">a roaring lion,</hi> hungry, fierce, strong, and cruel, the fierce and greedy pursuer of souls. <div eID="gen33525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33526" type="x-p"/> 2. By his business: <hi type="italic">He walks about, seeking whom he may devour;</hi> his whole design is to devour and destroy souls. To this end he is unwearied and restless in his malicious endeavours; for he always, night and day, goes about studying and contriving whom he may ensnare to their eternal ruin. <div eID="gen33526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33527" type="x-p"/> II. Hence he infers that it is their duty, 1. To <hi type="italic">be sober,</hi> and to govern both the outward and the inward man by the rules of temperance, modesty, and mortification. 2. To <hi type="italic">be vigilant;</hi> not secure or careless, but rather suspicious of constant danger from this spiritual enemy, and, under that apprehension, to be watchful and diligent to prevent his designs and save our souls. 3. To resist him <hi type="italic">stedfast in the faith.</hi> It was the faith of these people that Satan aimed at; if he could overturn their faith, and draw them into apostasy, then he knew he should gain his point, and ruin their souls; therefore, to destroy their faith, he raises bitter persecutions, and sets the grand potentates of the world against them. This strong trial and temptation they must resist, by being well-grounded, resolute, and stedfast in the faith: to encourage them to this, <div eID="gen33527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33528" type="x-p"/> III. He tells them that their care was not singular, for they knew that the like afflictions befel their brethren in all parts of the world, and that all the people of God were their fellow-soldiers in this warfare. Learn, 1. All the great persecutions that ever were in the world were raised, spirited up, and conducted, by the devil; he is the grand persecutor, as well as <hi type="italic">the deceiver and accuser, of the brethren;</hi> men are his willing spiteful instruments, but he is the chief adversary that wars against Christ and his people, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Gen. iii. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.12.12">Rev. xii. 12</reference>. 2. The design of Satan in raising persecutions against the faithful servants of God is to bring them to apostasy, by reason of their sufferings, and so to destroy their souls. 3. Sobriety and watchfulness are necessary virtues at all times, but especially in times of suffering and persecution. "You must moderate your affection to worldly things, or else Satan will soon overcome you." 4. "If you would overcome Satan, as a tempter, an accuser, or a persecutor, you must resist him stedfast in the faith; if your faith give way, you are gone; therefore, <hi type="italic">above all, take the shield of faith,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Eph.6.16">Eph. vi. 16</reference>. 5. The consideration of what others suffer is proper to encourage us to bear our own share in any affliction: <hi type="italic">The same afflictions are accomplished in your brethren.</hi>
entries.c8d50f32bbd36ff17433c24fb506971371e1bde3: <div eID="gen33528" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle's Prayer. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen33529" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> But the God of all grace, who hath called us unto his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, after that ye have suffered a while, make you perfect, stablish, strengthen, settle <hi type="italic">you.</hi> 11 To him <hi type="italic">be</hi> glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen. <hi type="super">12</hi> By Silvanus, a faithful brother unto you, as I suppose, I have written briefly, exhorting, and testifying that this is the true grace of God wherein ye stand. <hi type="super">13</hi> The <hi type="italic">church that is</hi> at Babylon, elected together with <hi type="italic">you,</hi> saluteth you; and <hi type="italic">so doth</hi> Marcus my son. <hi type="super">14</hi> Greet ye one another with a kiss of charity. Peace <hi type="italic">be</hi> with you all that are in Christ Jesus. Amen. <div eID="gen33529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33530" type="x-p"/> We come now to the conclusion of this epistle, which, <div eID="gen33530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33531" type="x-p"/> I. The apostle begins with a most weighty prayer, which he addresses to God as <hi type="italic">the God of all grace,</hi> the author and finisher of every heavenly gift and quality, acknowledging, on their behalf, that God had already called them to be partakers of that eternal glory, which, being his own, he had promised and settled upon them, through the merit and intercession of Jesus Christ. Observe, <div eID="gen33531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33532" type="x-p"/> 1. What he prays for on their account; not that they might be excused from sufferings, but that their sufferings might be moderate and short, and, <hi type="italic">after they had suffered awhile,</hi> that God would restore them to a settled and peaceable condition, and perfect his work in them—that he would establish them against wavering, either in faith or duty, that he would strengthen those who were weak, and settle them upon Christ the foundation, so firmly that their union with him might be indissoluble and everlasting. Learn, (1.) All grace is from God; it is he who restrains, converts, comforts, and saves men by his grace. (2.) All who are called into a state of grace are called to partake of eternal glory and happiness. (3.) Those who are called to be heirs of eternal life through Jesus Christ must, nevertheless, suffer in this world, but their sufferings will be but for a little while. (4.) The perfecting, establishing, strengthening, and settling, of good people in grace, and their perseverance therein, is so difficult a work, that only the God of all grace can accomplish it; and therefore he is earnestly to be sought unto by continual prayer, and dependence upon his promises. <div eID="gen33532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33533" type="x-p"/> 2. His doxology, <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.11">v. 11</reference>. From this doxology we may learn that those who have obtained grace from the God of all grace should and will ascribe glory, dominion, and power, to him for ever and ever. <div eID="gen33533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33534" type="x-p"/> II. He recapitulates the design of his writing this epistle to them (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.12">v. 12</reference>), which was, 1. To testify, and in the strongest terms to assure them, that the doctrine of salvation, which he had explained and they had embraced, was the true account of the grace of God, foretold by the prophets and published by Jesus Christ. 2. To exhort them earnestly that, as they had embraced the gospel, they would continue stedfast in it, notwithstanding the arts of seducers, or the persecutions of enemies. (1.) The main thing that ministers ought to aim at in their labours is to convince their people of the certainty and excellency of the Christian religion; this the apostles did <hi type="italic">exhort and testify</hi> with all their might. (2.) A firm persuasion that we are in the true way to heaven will be the best motive to stand fast, and persevere therein. <div eID="gen33534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33535" type="x-p"/> III. He recommends <hi type="italic">Silvanus,</hi> the person by whom he sent them this brief epistle, as a brother whom he esteemed faithful and friendly to them, and hoped they would account him so, though he was a ministers of the uncircumcision. Observe, An honourable esteem of the ministers of religion tends much to the success of their labours. When we are convinced they are faithful, we shall profit more by their ministerial services. The prejudices that some of these Jews might have against Silvanus, as a minister of the Gentiles, would soon wear off when they were once convinced that he was a faithful brother. <div eID="gen33535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33536" type="x-p"/> IV. He closes with salutations and a solemn benediction. Observe, 1. Peter, being at Babylon in Assyria, when he wrote this epistle (whither he travelled, as the apostle of the circumcision, to visit that church, which was the chief of the dispersion), sends the salutation of that church to the other churches to whom he wrote (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.13">v. 13</reference>), telling them that God had <hi type="italic">elected</hi> or chosen the Christians at Babylon out of the world, to be his church, and to partake of eternal salvation through Christ Jesus, together with them and all other faithful Christians, <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.2">ch. i. 2</reference>. In this salutation he particularly joins Mark the evangelist, who was then with him, and who was his son in a spiritual sense, being begotten by him to Christianity. Observe, All the churches of Jesus Christ ought to have a most affectionate concern one for another; they should love and pray for one another, and be as helpful one to another as they possibly can. 2. He exhorts them to fervent love and charity one towards another, and to express this by giving <hi type="italic">the kiss of peace</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.14">v. 14</reference>), according to the common custom of those times and countries, and so concludes with a benediction, which he confines to those <hi type="italic">that are in Christ Jesus,</hi> united to him by faith and sound members of his mystical body. The blessing he pronounces upon them is <hi type="italic">peace,</hi> by which he means all necessary good, all manner of prosperity; to this he adds his <hi type="italic">amen,</hi> in token of his earnest desire and undoubted expectation that the blessing of peace would be the portion of all the faithful.  <chapter eID="1Pet.5"/> <div eID="gen33536" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen33336" osisID="1Pet" type="book"/>

entries.057e2f9e781ea00dfd2527fad424871868ffc185: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18818"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 5</title> <div sID="gen40167" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.1-1Pet.5.14">1Pe 5:1-14</reference>. Exhortations to Elders, Juniors, and All in General. Parting Prayer. Conclusion.<div eID="gen40167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40168" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18818"/><hi type="bold">1. elders--</hi>alike in office and age (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.5">1Pe 5:5</reference>).<div eID="gen40168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40169" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I ... also an elder--</hi>To put one's self on a level with those whom we exhort, gives weight to one's exhortations (compare <reference osisRef="2John.1.2">2Jo 1, 2</reference>). Peter, in true humility for the Gospel's sake, does not put forward his apostleship here, wherein he presided over the elders. In the apostleship the apostles have no successors, for "the signs of an apostle" have not been transmitted. The presidents over the presbyters and deacons, by whatever name designated, angel, bishop, or moderator, &c., though of the same ORDER as the presbyters, yet have virtually succeeded to a superintendency of the Church analogous to that exercised by the apostles (this superintendency and priority existed from the earliest times after the apostles [Tertullian]); just as the Jewish synagogue (the model which the Church followed) was governed by a council of presbyters, presided over by one of themselves, "the chief ruler of the synagogue." (Compare Vitringa [Synagogue and Temple, Part II, chs. 3 and 7]).<div eID="gen40169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40170" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">witness--</hi>an eye-witness of Christ's sufferings, and so qualified to exhort you to believing patience in suffering for well-doing after His example (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.19">1Pe 4:19</reference>; 2:20). This explains the "therefore" inserted in the oldest manuscripts, "I therefore exhort," resuming exhortation from <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.19">1Pe 4:19</reference>. His higher dignity as an apostle is herein delicately implied, as eye-witnessing was a necessary qualification for apostleship: compare Peter's own speeches, <reference osisRef="Acts.1.21">Ac 1:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.22">22</reference>; 2:32; 10:39.<div eID="gen40170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40171" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">also--</hi>implying the righteous recompense corresponding to the sufferings.<div eID="gen40171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40172" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">partaker of the glory--</hi>according to Christ's promise; an earnest of which was given in the transfiguration. <div eID="gen40172" type="x-p"/>
entries.a5636d336efae0fa943f3237778bdb29b1205a71: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18819"/><div sID="gen40173" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18819"/><hi type="bold">2. Feed--</hi>Greek, "Tend as a shepherd," by discipline and doctrine. Lead, feed, heed: by prayer, exhortation, government, and example. The dignity is marked by the term "elder"; the duties of the office, to tend or oversee, by "bishop." Peter has in mind Christ's injunction to him, "Feed (tend) My sheep ... Feed (pasture) My lambs" (<reference osisRef="John.21.16">Joh 21:16</reference>). He invites the elders to share with him the same duty (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.20.28">Ac 20:28</reference>). The flock is Christ's.<div eID="gen40173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40174" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which is among you--</hi>While having a concern for all the Church, your special duty is to feed that portion of it "which is among you."<div eID="gen40174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40175" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">oversight--</hi>Greek, "bishopric," or duty of bishops, that is, overseer.<div eID="gen40175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40176" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not by constraint--</hi>Necessity is laid upon them, but willingness prevents it being felt, both in undertaking and in fulfilling the duty [Bengel]. "He is a true presbyter and minister of the counsel of God who doeth and teacheth the things of the Lord, being not accounted righteous merely because he is a presbyter, but because righteous, chosen into the presbytery" [Clement of Alexandria].<div eID="gen40176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40177" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">willingly--</hi>One oldest manuscript, Vulgate, Syriac, and Coptic, add, "as God would have it to be done" (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.27">Ro 8:27</reference>).<div eID="gen40177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40178" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not for filthy lucre--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.56.11">Is 56:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.7">Tit 1:7</reference>).<div eID="gen40178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40179" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of a ready mind--</hi>promptly and heartily, without selfish motive of gain-seeking, as the Israelites gave their services willing-heartedly to the sanctuary. <div eID="gen40179" type="x-p"/>
entries.aaae7edbb465f070056679e427389586b766af03: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18820"/><div sID="gen40180" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18820"/><hi type="bold">3. being lords--</hi>Greek, "lording it": implying pride and oppression. "Not that we have dominion over your faith."<div eID="gen40180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40181" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God's heritage--</hi>Greek, "the inheritances," that is, the portions of the Church committed severally to your pastoral charge [Bengel]. It is explained by "the flock" in the next clause. However, in <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.2">1Pe 5:2</reference>, "flock of God which is among you," answering to "(God's) heritages" (plural to express the sheep who are God's portion and inheritance, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.9">De 32:9</reference>) committed to you, favors English Version. The flock, as one whole, is God's heritage, or flock in the singular. Regarded in relation to its component sheep, divided among several pastors, it is in the plural "heritages." Compare <reference osisRef="Acts.1.17">Ac 1:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.25">25</reference>, "part" (the same Greek). Bernard of Clairvaux, wrote to Pope Eugene, "Peter could not give thee what he had not: what he had he gave: the care over the Church, not dominion."<div eID="gen40181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40182" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">being--</hi>Greek, "becoming."<div eID="gen40182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40183" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ensamples--</hi>the most effective recommendation of precept (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.12">1Ti 4:12</reference>). <reference osisRef="Titus.2.7">Tit 2:7</reference>, "patterns." So Jesus. "A monstrosity it is to see the highest rank joined with the meanest mind, the first seat with the lowest life, a grandiloquent tongue with a lazy life, much talking with no fruit" [Bernard]. <div eID="gen40183" type="x-p"/>
entries.6c7eaa1743aacc567333c7cf5852928020601b1e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18821"/><div sID="gen40184" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18821"/><hi type="bold">4. And--</hi>"And so": as the result of "being ensamples" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.3">1Pe 5:3</reference>).<div eID="gen40184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40185" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chief Shepherd--</hi>the title peculiarly Christ's own, not Peter's or the pope's.<div eID="gen40185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40186" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when ... shall appear--</hi>Greek, "be manifested" (<reference osisRef="Col.3.4">Col 3:4</reference>). Faith serves the Lord while still unseen.<div eID="gen40186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40187" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">crown--</hi>Greek, "stephanos," a garland of victory, the prize in the Grecian games, woven of ivy, parsley, myrtle, olive, or oak. Our crown is distinguished from theirs in that it is "incorruptible" and "fadeth not away," as the leaves of theirs soon did. "The crown of life." Not a kingly "crown" (a different Greek word, diadema): the prerogative of the Lord Jesus (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.12">Re 19:12</reference>).<div eID="gen40187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40188" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">glory--</hi>Greek, "the glory," namely, to be then revealed (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.1">1Pe 5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.13">1Pe 4:13</reference>).<div eID="gen40188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40189" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that fadeth not away--</hi>Greek, "amaranthine" (compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.4">1Pe 1:4</reference>). <div eID="gen40189" type="x-p"/>
entries.8887a392126d66983da9f4c015e84fc2dce5116e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18822"/><div sID="gen40190" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18822"/><hi type="bold">5. ye younger--</hi>The deacons were originally the younger men, the presbyters older; but subsequently as presbyter expressed the office of Church ruler or teacher, so Greek "neoteros" means not (as literally) young men in age, but subordinate ministers and servants of the Church. So Christ uses the term "younger." For He explains it by "he that doth serve," literally, "he that ministereth as a deacon"; just as He explains "the greatness" by "he that is chief," literally, "he that ruleth," the very word applied to the bishops or presbyters. So "the young men" are undoubtedly the deacons of the Church of Jerusalem, of whom, as being all Hebrews, the Hellenistic Christians subsequently complained as neglecting their Grecian widows, whence arose the appointment of the seven others, Hellenistic deacons. So here, Peter, having exhorted the presbyters, or elders, not to lord it over those committed to them, adds, Likewise ye neoters or younger, that is, subordinate ministers and deacons, submit cheerfully to the command of the elders [Mosheim]. There is no Scripture sanction for "younger" meaning laymen in general (as Alford explains): its use in this sense is probably of later date. The "all of you" that follows, refers to the congregation generally; and it is likely that, like Paul, Peter should notice, previous to the general congregation, the subordinate ministers as well as the presbyters, writing as he did to the same region (Ephesus), and to confirm the teaching of the apostle of the Gentiles.<div eID="gen40190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40191" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Yea--</hi>to sum up all my exhortations in one.<div eID="gen40191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40192" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be subject--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts and versions, but Tischendorf quotes the Vatican manuscript for it. Then translate, "Gird (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.13">1Pe 1:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.1">4:1</reference>) fast on humility (lowliness of mind) to one another." The verb is literally, "tie on with a fast knot" [Wahl]. Or, "gird on humility as the slave dress (encomboma)": as the Lord girded Himself with a towel to perform a servile office of humility and love, washing His disciples' feet, a scene in which Peter had played an important part, so that he would naturally have it before his mind. Compare similarly <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.2">1Pe 5:2</reference> with <reference osisRef="John.21.15-John.21.17">Joh 21:15-17</reference>. Clothing was the original badge of man's sin and shame. Pride caused the need of man's clothing, and pride still reigns in dress; the Christian therefore clothes himself in humility (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.3">1Pe 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.4">4</reference>). God provides him with the robe of Christ's righteousness, in order to receive which man must be stripped of pride.<div eID="gen40192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40193" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God resisteth the proud--</hi>Quoted, as <reference osisRef="Jas.4.6">Jas 4:6</reference>, from <reference osisRef="Prov.3.34">Pr 3:34</reference>. Peter had James before his mind, and gives his Epistle inspired sanction. Compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.9">1Pe 5:9</reference> with <reference osisRef="Jas.4.7">Jas 4:7</reference>, literally, "arrayeth Himself against." Other sins flee from God: pride alone opposeth itself to God; therefore, God also in turn opposes Himself to the proud [Gerhard in Alford]. Humility is the vessel of all graces [Augustine]. <div eID="gen40193" type="x-p"/>
entries.bef9d7bb50bb97f470a9b880f69ce063a27862b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18823"/><div sID="gen40194" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18823"/><hi type="bold">6. under the mighty hand--</hi>afflicting you (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.15">1Pe 3:15</reference>): "accept" His chastisements, and turn to Him that smiteth you. He depresses the proud and exalts the humble.<div eID="gen40194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40195" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in due time--</hi>Wait humbly and patiently for His own fit time. One oldest manuscript and Vulgate read, "In the season of visitation," namely, His visitation in mercy. <div eID="gen40195" type="x-p"/>
entries.07a291af7478ae6acd97b1d9e460e434494a374d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18824"/><div sID="gen40196" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18824"/><hi type="bold">7. Casting--</hi>once for all: so the Greek aorist.<div eID="gen40196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40197" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">care--</hi>"anxiety? The advantage flowing from humbling ourselves under God's hand (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.6">1Pe 5:6</reference>) is confident reliance on His goodness. Exemption from care goes along with humble submission to God.<div eID="gen40197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40198" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">careth for you--</hi>literally "respecting you." Care is a burden which faith casts off the man on his God. Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.22.10">Psa 22:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.5">37:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.55.22">55:22</reference>, to which Peter alludes; <reference osisRef="Luke.12.22">Lu 12:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.37">37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.4.6">Php 4:6</reference>.<div eID="gen40198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40199" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">careth--</hi>not so strong a Greek word as the previous Greek "anxiety." <div eID="gen40199" type="x-p"/>
entries.6fc7fc737e6b1d49a44e3c760d321b5ea3c8fb24: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18825"/><div sID="gen40200" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18825"/>8. Peter has in mind Christ's warning to himself to watch against Satan, from forgetting which he fell.<div eID="gen40200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40201" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Be sober ... vigilant--</hi>"Care," that is, anxiety, will intoxicate the soul; therefore be sober, that is, self-restrained. Yet, lest this freedom from care should lead any to false security, he adds, "Be vigilant" against "your adversary." Let this be your "care." God provides, therefore do not be anxious. The devil seeks, therefore watch [Bengel].<div eID="gen40201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40202" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts The broken and disjointed sentences are more fervid and forcible. Lucifer of Cagliari reads as English Version.<div eID="gen40202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40203" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">adversary--</hi>literally, "opponent in a court of justice" (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.1">Zec 3:1</reference>). "Satan" means opponent. "Devil," accuser or slanderer (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.10">Re 12:10</reference>). "The enemy" (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.39">Mt 13:39</reference>). "A murderer from the beginning" (<reference osisRef="John.8.44">Joh 8:44</reference>). He counteracts the Gospel and its agents. "The tempter."<div eID="gen40203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40204" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">roaring lion--</hi>implying his violent and insatiable thirst for prey as a hungry lion. Through man's sin he got God's justice on his side against us; but Christ, our Advocate, by fulfilling all the demands of justice for us, has made our redemption altogether consistent with justice.<div eID="gen40204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40205" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">walketh about--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.1.7">Job 1:7</reference>; 2:2). So the children of the wicked one cannot rest. Evil spirits are in <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.4">2Pe 2:4</reference>; Jude 6, said to be already in chains of darkness and in hell. This probably means that this is their doom finally: a doom already begun in part; though for a time they are permitted to roam in the world (of which Satan is prince), especially in the dark air that surrounds the earth. Hence perhaps arises the miasma of the air at times, as physical and moral evil are closely connected.<div eID="gen40205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40206" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">devour--</hi>entangle in worldly "care" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.7">1Pe 5:7</reference>) and other snares, so as finally to destroy. Compare <reference osisRef="Rev.12.15">Re 12:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.12.16">16</reference>. <div eID="gen40206" type="x-p"/>
entries.d81b6157f150aab72a7d887145b7622c64c7c6f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18826"/><div sID="gen40207" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18826"/>9. (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.13">Lu 4:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.6.11-Eph.6.17">Ep 6:11-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.7">Jas 4:7</reference>.)<div eID="gen40207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40208" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">steadfast--</hi>Compare established in the truth," <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.12">2Pe 1:12</reference>. Satan's power exists only in respect to the unbelieving; the faithful he cannot hurt (<reference osisRef="1John.5.18">1Jo 5:18</reference>). Faith gives strength to prayer, the great instrument against the foe (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.6">Jas 1:6</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen40208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40209" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knowing, &c.--</hi>"encouragement not to faint in afflictions": your brethren suffer the same; nothing beyond the common lot of Christians befalls you (<reference osisRef="1Cor.10.13">1Co 10:13</reference>). It is a sign of God's favor rather than displeasure, that Satan is allowed to harass you, as he did Job. Your fellow Christians have the same battle of faith and prayer against Satan.<div eID="gen40209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40210" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are--</hi>are being accomplished according to the appointment of God.<div eID="gen40210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40211" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the world--</hi>lying in the wicked one, and therefore necessarily the scene of "tribulation" (<reference osisRef="John.16.33">Joh 16:33</reference>). <div eID="gen40211" type="x-p"/>
entries.d60af608619961112cfb9dbea36a5f8a7105bc29: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18827"/><div sID="gen40212" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18827"/>10. Comforting assurance that God will finally "perfect" His work of "grace" in them, after they have undergone the necessary previous suffering.<div eID="gen40212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40213" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">But--</hi>Only do you watch and resist the foe: God will perform the rest [Bengel].<div eID="gen40213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40214" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of all grace--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.10">1Pe 4:10</reference>). The God to whom as its source all grace is to be referred; who in grace completes what in grace He began. He from the first "called (so the oldest manuscripts read for "us") unto (with a view to) glory." He will not let His purpose fall short of completion. If He does so in punishing, much more in grace. The three are fitly conjoined: the call, the glory to which we are called, and the way (suffering); the fourth is the ground of the calling, namely, the grace of God in Christ.<div eID="gen40214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40215" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by--</hi>Greek, "in." Christ is He in virtue of whom, and in union with whom, believers are called to glory. The opposite is "in the world" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.9">1Pe 5:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.33">Joh 16:33</reference>).<div eID="gen40215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40216" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after that ye have suffered--</hi>Join to "called you": suffering, as a necessary preliminary to glory, was contemplated in God's calling.<div eID="gen40216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40217" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a while--</hi>short and inconsiderable, as compared with the glory.<div eID="gen40217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40218" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">perfect, &c.--</hi>The two oldest manuscripts, and Vulgate and Coptic versions, read, "shall perfect (so that there shall be nothing defective in you), stablish, strengthen," and omit "settle," literally, "ground," or "fix on a foundation." Alford reads it in spite of the oldest manuscripts The authority of the latter I prefer; moreover the climax seems to require rather a verb of completing the work of grace, than, as the Greek means, founding it. The Greek has, "shall HIMSELF perfect you": though you are called on to watch and resist the foe, God Himself must really do all in and through you. The same God who begins must Himself complete the work. The Greek for "stablish" (so as to be "steadfast in the faith," <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.9">1Pe 5:9</reference>) is the same as "strengthen," <reference osisRef="Luke.22.32">Lu 22:32</reference>. Peter has in mind Christ's charge, "When thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren." His exhortation accords with his name Peter, "Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build My Church." "Stablish," so as not to waver. "Strengthen" with might in the inner man by His Spirit, against the foe. <div eID="gen40218" type="x-p"/>
entries.933d7ea1fb0897255d1cfe43f1c77ef5de57378d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18828"/><div sID="gen40219" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18828"/><hi type="bold">11. To him--</hi>emphatic. To Him and Him alone: not to ourselves. Compare "Himself," see on <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.10">1Pe 5:10</reference>.<div eID="gen40219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40220" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">glory and--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts and versions.<div eID="gen40220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40221" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dominion--</hi>Greek, "the might" shown in so "perfecting," you, <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.10">1Pe 5:10</reference>. <div eID="gen40221" type="x-p"/>
entries.c0d2357fb6daa64109ec766e00e1492921b7efb3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18829"/><div sID="gen40222" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18829"/><hi type="bold">12. Silvanus--</hi>Silas, the companion of Paul and Timothy: a suitable messenger by whom to confirm, as Peter here does, Paul's doctrine of "the true grace of God" in the same churches (compare <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.16">2Pe 3:16</reference>). We never meet with Silvanus as Paul's companion after Paul's last journey to Jerusalem. His connection with Peter was plainly subsequent to that journey.<div eID="gen40222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40223" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as I suppose--</hi>Join "faithful unto you [Steiger], as I suppose." Silvanus may have stood in a close relation to the churches in Asia, perhaps having taken the oversight of them after Paul's departure, and had afterwards gone to Peter, by whom he is now sent back to them with this Epistle. He did not know, by positive observation, Silvanus' faithfulness to them; he therefore says, "faithful to you, as I suppose," from the accounts I hear; not expressing doubt. Alford joins "I have written unto you," which the Greek order favors. The seeming uncertainty, thus, is not as to Silvanus' faithfulness, which strongly marked by the Greek article, but as to whether he or some other would prove to be the bearer of the letter, addressed as it was to five provinces, all of which Silvanus might not reach: "By Silvanus, that faithful brother, as expect, I have Written to you" [Birks].<div eID="gen40223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40224" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">briefly--</hi>Greek, "in few (words)," as compared with the importance of the subject (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.22">He 13:22</reference>).<div eID="gen40224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40225" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">exhorting--</hi>not so much formally teaching doctrines, which could not be done in so "few words."<div eID="gen40225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40226" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">testifying--</hi>bearing my testimony in confirmation (so the Greek compound verb implies) of that truth which ye have already heard from Paul and Silas (<reference osisRef="1John.2.27">1Jo 2:27</reference>).<div eID="gen40226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40227" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that this--</hi>of which I have just written, and of which Paul before testified to you (whose testimony, now that he was no longer in those regions, was called in question probably by some; compare <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.15">2Pe 3:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.16">16</reference>). <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.12">2Pe 1:12</reference>, "the present truth," namely, the grace formerly promised by the prophets, and now manifested to you. "Grace" is the keynote of Paul's doctrine which Peter now confirms (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.5">Ep 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.8">8</reference>). Their sufferings for the Gospel made them to need some attestation and confirmation of the truth, that they should not fall back from it.<div eID="gen40227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40228" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wherein ye stand--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read imperatively, "Stand ye." Literally, "into which (having been already admitted, <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.8">1Pe 1:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.8">2:7, 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.9">9</reference>) stand (therein)." Peter seems to have in mind Paul's words (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.2">Ro 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.1">1Co 15:1</reference>). "The grace wherein we stand must be true, and our standing in it true also" [Bengel]. Compare in "He began his Epistle with grace (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.2">1Pe 1:2</reference>), he finishes it with grace, he has besprinkled the middle with grace, that in every part he might teach that the Church is not saved but by grace." <div eID="gen40228" type="x-p"/>
entries.4bdb2dc43cafdfa0a7f10964d60ec5948cab8148: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18830"/><div sID="gen40229" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18830"/><hi type="bold">13. The ... at Babylon--</hi>Alford, Bengel, and others translate, "She that is elected together with you in Babylon," namely, Peter's wife, whom he led about with him in his missionary journeys. Compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.7">1Pe 3:7</reference>, "heirs together of the grace of life." But why she should be called "elected together with you in Babylon," as if there had been no Christian woman in Babylon besides, is inexplicable on this view. In English Version the sense is clear: "That portion of the whole dispersion (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.1">1Pe 1:1</reference>, Greek), or Church of Christianized Jews, with Gentile converts, which resides in Babylon." As Peter and John were closely associated, Peter addresses the Church in John's peculiar province, Asia, and closes with "your co-elect sister Church at Babylon saluteth you"; and John similarly addresses the "elect lady," that is, the Church in Babylon, and closes with "the children of thine elect sister (the Asiatic Church) greet thee"; (compare Introduction to Second John). Erasmus explains, "Mark who is in the place of a son to me": compare <reference osisRef="Acts.12.12">Ac 12:12</reference>, implying Peter's connection with Mark; whence the mention of him in connection with the Church at Babylon, in which he labored under Peter before he went to Alexandria is not unnatural. Papias reports from the presbyter John [Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, 3.39], that Mark was interpreter of Peter, recording in his Gospel the facts related to him by Peter. Silvanus or Silas had been substituted for John Mark, as Paul's companion, because of Mark's temporary unfaithfulness. But now Mark restored is associated with Silvanus, Paul's companion, in Peter's esteem, as Mark was already reinstated in Paul's esteem. That Mark had a spiritual connection with the Asiatic' churches which Peter addresses, and so naturally salutes them, appears from <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.11">2Ti 4:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.4.10">Col 4:10</reference>.<div eID="gen40229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40230" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Babylon--</hi>The Chaldean Babylon on the Euphrates. See Introduction, ON THE PLACE OF WRITING this Epistle, in proof that Rome is not meant as Papists assert; compare Lightfoot sermon. How unlikely that in a friendly salutation the enigmatical title of Rome given in prophecy (John, <reference osisRef="Rev.17.5">Re 17:5</reference>), should be used! Babylon was the center from which the Asiatic dispersion whom Peter addresses was derived. Philo [The Embassy to Gaius, 36] and Josephus [Antiquities, 15.2.2; 23.12] inform us that Babylon contained a great many Jews in the apostolic age (whereas those at Rome were comparatively few, about eight thousand [Josephus, Antiquities, 17.11]); so it would naturally be visited by the apostle of the circumcision. It was the headquarters of those whom he had so successfully addressed on Pentecost, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.9">Ac 2:9</reference>, Jewish "Parthians ... dwellers in Mesopotamia" (the Parthians were then masters of Mesopotamian Babylon); these he ministered to in person. His other hearers, the Jewish "dwellers in Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia, Pamphylia," he now ministers to by letter. The earliest distinct authority for Peter's martyrdom at Rome is Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, in the latter half of the second century. The desirableness of representing Peter and Paul, the two leading apostles, as together founding the Church of the metropolis, seems to have originated the tradition. Clement of Rome [First Epistle to the Corinthians, 4.5], often quoted for, is really against it. He mentions Paul and Peter together, but makes it as a distinguishing circumstance of Paul, that he preached both in the East and West, implying that Peter never was in the West. In <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.14">2Pe 1:14</reference>, he says, "I must shortly put off this tabernacle," implying his martyrdom was near, yet he makes no allusion to Rome, or any intention of his visiting it. <div eID="gen40230" type="x-p"/>
entries.492a732cf40cbb0b822013676e0fb9d5c639385b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18831"/><div sID="gen40231" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18831"/><hi type="bold">14. kiss of charity--</hi><reference osisRef="Rom.16.16">Ro 16:16</reference>, "an holy kiss": the token of love to God and the brethren. Love and holiness are inseparable. Compare the instance, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.37">Ac 20:37</reference>.<div eID="gen40231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40232" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Peace--</hi>Peter's closing salutation; as Paul's is, "Grace be with you," though he accompanies it with "peace be to the brethren." "Peace" (flowing from salvation) was Christ's own salutation after the resurrection, and from Him Peter derives it.<div eID="gen40232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40233" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be with you all that are in Christ Jesus--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit "Jesus." In <reference osisRef="Eph.6.24">Ep 6:24</reference>, addressed to the same region, the same limitation of the salutation occurs, whence, perhaps, Peter here adopts it. Contrast, "Be with you all," <reference osisRef="Rom.16.24">Ro 16:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.23">1Co 16:23</reference>. <chapter eID="1Pet.5"/><div eID="gen40233" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen39736" osisID="1Pet" type="book"/>

entries.83f95e49b0b97624270ea47d1abd38749fc71575: <div eID="gen54705" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen54706" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen54707" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen54707" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen54706" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen54708" type="x-p"/> Directions to the elders to feed the flock of God, and not to be lord over God's heritage, that when the chief Shepherd does appear, they may receive a crown of glory, <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.1-1Pet.5.4">1Pet 5:1-4</reference>. The young are to submit themselves to the elder, and to humble themselves under the mighty hand of God, and cast all their care upon him, <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.5-1Pet.5.7">1Pet 5:5-7</reference>. They should be sober and watchful, because their adversary the devil is continually seeking their destruction, whom they are to resist, steadfast in the faith, <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.8">1Pet 5:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.9">1Pet 5:9</reference>. They are informed that the God of all grace had called them to his eternal glory, <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.10-1Pet.5.11">1Pet 5:10-11</reference>. Of Silvanus, by whom this epistle was sent, <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.12">1Pet 5:12</reference>. Salutations from the Church at Babylon, <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.13">1Pet 5:13</reference>. The apostolic benediction, <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.14">1Pet 5:14</reference>. <div eID="gen54708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54709" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen54709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54710" type="x-p"/> The elders which are among you - In this place the term πρεσβυτεροι, elders or presbyters is the name of an office. They were as pastors or shepherds of the flock of God, the Christian people among whom they lived. They were the same as bishops, presidents, teachers and deacons, <reference osisRef="Act.14.23">Act 14:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.17">1Tim 5:17</reference>. And that these were the same as bishops the next verse proves. <div eID="gen54710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54711" type="x-p"/> Who am also an elder - Συμπρεσβυτερος· A fellow elder; one on a level with yourselves. Had he been what the popes of Rome say he was - the prince of the apostles; and head of the Church, and what they affect to be - mighty secular lords, binding the kings of the earth in chains, and their nobles in fetters of iron; could he have spoken of himself as he here does? It is true that the Roman pontiffs, in all their bulls, each style themselves servus servorum Dei, servant of the servants of God, while each affects to be rex regum, king of kings, and vicar of Jesus Christ. But the popes and the Scriptures never agree. <div eID="gen54711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54712" type="x-p"/> A witness of the sufferings of Christ - He was with Christ in the garden; he was with him when he was apprehended. and he was with him in the high priest's hall. Whether he followed him to the cross we know not; probably he did not, for in the hall of the high priest he had denied him most shamefully; and, having been deeply convinced of the greatness of his crime, it is likely he withdrew to some private place, to humble himself before God, and to implore mercy. He could, however, with the strictest propriety, say, from the above circumstances, that he was a witness of the sufferings of Christ. <div eID="gen54712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54713" type="x-p"/> A partaker of the glory - He had a right to it through the blood of the Lamb; he had a blessed anticipation of it by the power of the Holy Ghost; and he had the promise from his Lord and Master that he should be with him in heaven, to behold his glory; <reference osisRef="Joh.17.21">Joh 17:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.17.24">Joh 17:24</reference>.
entries.20fc88b4fb6c72c9a0b398eaa42f53f813d77e58: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen54713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54714" type="x-p"/> Feed the flock - Do not fleece the flock. <div eID="gen54714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54715" type="x-p"/> Taking the oversight - Επισκοπουντες· Discharging the office of bishops or superintendents. This is another proof that bishop and presbyter were the same order in the apostolic times, though afterwards they were made distinct. <div eID="gen54715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54716" type="x-p"/> Not by constraint - The office was laborious and dangerous, especially in these times of persecution; it is no wonder then that even those who were best qualified for the office should strive to excuse themselves with a genuine Nolo episcopari, "I am unwilling to be a bishop." <div eID="gen54716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54717" type="x-p"/> Not for filthy lucre - Could the office of a bishop, in those early days, and in the time of persecution, be a lucrative office? Does not the Spirit of God lead the apostle to speak these things rather for posterity than for that time? See the notes on <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.3">1Tim 3:3</reference>. <div eID="gen54717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54718" type="x-p"/> But of a ready mind - Doing all for Christ's sake, and through love to immortal souls.
entries.824d78305bf1c93dda55dc3f56793be629535fad: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen54718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54719" type="x-p"/> Neither as being lords over God's heritage - This is the voice of St. Peter in his catholic epistle to the catholic Church! According to him there are to be no lords over God's heritage, the bishops and presbyters who are appointed by the head of the Church are to feed the flock, to guide and to defend it, not to fleece and waste it; and they are to look for their reward in another world, and in the approbation of God in their consciences. And in humility, self-abasement, self-renunciation, and heavenly-mindedness, they are to be ensamples, τυποι, types, to the flock, moulds of a heavenly form, into which the spirits and lives of the flock may be cast, that they may come out after a perfect pattern. We need not ask, Does the Church that arrogates to itself the exclusive title of Catholic, and do its supreme pastors, who affect to be the successors of Peter and the vicars of Jesus Christ, act in this way? They are in every sense the reverse of this. But we may ask, Do the other Churches, which profess to be reformed from the abominations of the above, keep the advice of the apostle in their eye? Have they pastors according to God's own heart, who feed them with knowledge and understanding? <reference osisRef="Jer.3.15">Jer 3:15</reference>. Do they feed themselves, and not the flock? Are they lords over the heritage of Christ, ruling with a high eclesiastico-secular hand, disputing with their flocks about penny-farthing tithes and stipends, rather than contending for the faith once delivered to the saints? Are they heavenly moulds, into which the spirits and conduct of their flocks may be cast? I leave those who are concerned to answer these questions; but I put them, in the name of God, to all the preachers in the land. How many among them properly care for the flock? Even among those reputed evangelical teachers, are there not some who, on their first coming to a parish or a congregation, make it their first business to raise the tithes and the stipends, where, in all good conscience, there was before enough, and more than enough, to provide them and their families with not only the necessaries, but all the conveniences and comforts of life? conveniences and comforts which neither Jesus Christ nor his servant Peter ever enjoyed. And is not the great concern among ministers to seek for those places, parishes, and congregations, where the provision is the most ample, and the work the smallest? Preacher or minister, whosoever thou art, who readest this, apply not the word to thy neighbor, whether he be state-appointed, congregation-appointed, or self-appointed; take all to thyself; mutato nomine de Te fabula narratur. See that thy own heart, views, and conduct be right with God; and then proceed to the next verse.
entries.aa3142bf41b93fe9a8974454149bf17fa405b862: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen54719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54720" type="x-p"/> When the chief Shepherd - That is, the Lord Jesus Christ, whose is the flock, and who provides the pasture, and from whom, if ye are legally called to the most awful work of preaching the Gospel, ye have received your commission; when he shall appear to judge the world in righteousness, ye who have fed his flock, who have taken the superintendency of it, not by constraint, nor for filthy lucre's sake, not as lords over the heritage, but with a ready mind, employing body, soul, spirit, time and talents, in endeavoring to pluck sinners as brands from eternal burnings, and build up the Church of Christ on its most holy faith; Ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away, an eternal nearness and intimacy with the ineffably glorious God; so that ye who have turned many to righteousness shall shine, not merely as stars, but as suns in the kingdom of your Father! O ye heavenly-minded, diligent, self-denying pastors after God's own heart, whether ye be in the Church established by the state, or in those divisions widely separated from, or nearly connected with it, take courage; preach Jesus; press through all difficulties in the faith of your God; fear no evil while meditating nothing but good. Ye are stars in the right hand of Jesus, who walks among your golden candlesticks, and has lighted that lamp of life which ye are appointed to trim; fear not, your labor in the Lord cannot be in vain! Never, never can ye preach one sermon in the spirit of your office, which the God of all grace shall permit to be unfruitful; ye carry and sow the seed of the kingdom by the command and on the authority of your God; ye sow it, and the heavens shall drop down dew upon it. Ye may go forth weeping, though bearing this precious seed; but ye shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing your sheaves with you. Amen, even so, Lord Jesus!
entries.487814ae5bc558fc6e165eb72ed63e3ade4999ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen54720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54721" type="x-p"/> Likewise, ye younger - Νεωτεροι probably means here inferiors, or those not in sacred offices; and may be understood as referring to the people at large who are called to obey them that have the rule over them in the Lord. In this sense our Lord, it appears, uses the word, <reference osisRef="Luk.22.26">Luk 22:26</reference>. <div eID="gen54721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54722" type="x-p"/> Be subject one to another - Strive all to serve each other; let the pastors strive to serve the people, and the people the pastors; and let there be no contention, but who shall do most to oblige and profit all the rest. <div eID="gen54722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54723" type="x-p"/> Be clothed with humility - To be clothed with a thing or person is a Greek mode of speech for being that thing or person with which a man is said to be clothed. Be ye truly humble; and let your outward garb and conduct be a proof of the humility of your hearts. Εγκομβωμα, from the original word εγκομβωσασθε, signifies often an outward ornamental garment, tied in different places with knots or bows, probably ornamented all over with bows or knots of different coloured ribands, silk twist, etc. But it also signifies the outward garment worn by servants, slaves, girls, and shepherds, which was rather intended to be the guard of the other garments than an ornament to those thus dressed: and I am rather inclined to take it in this sense than in the former; for as the apostle calls upon them to be subject to each other, he desires them to put on humility, as the encomboma or servant's dress, that they may appear to be such as were ready to serve; and that he cannot refer to this article of clothing as an ornament the next words sufficiently prove: God resisteth the Proud, and giveth grace to the Humble - the proud, with all their ornaments, God resists; while those who are clothed with the humble garment he adorns.
entries.6f912206e9d4aaf0d6f91713de4e31b4de96eb53: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen54723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54724" type="x-p"/> Humble yourselves - Those who submit patiently to the dispensations of God's providence he lifts up; those who lift themselves up, God thrusts down. <div eID="gen54724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54725" type="x-p"/> If we humble not ourselves under God's grace, he will humble us under his judgments. Those who patiently submit to him, he exalts in due time; if his hand be mighty to depress, it is also mighty to exalt.
entries.412eb6363685b275fcb3de7870fd11286982c480: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen54725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54726" type="x-p"/> Casting all your care - Την μεριμναν· Your anxiety, your distracting care, on him, for he careth for you, ὁτι αυτω μελει περι ὑμων, for he meddles or concerns himself, with the things that interest you. Whatever things concern a follower of God, whether they be spiritual or temporal, or whether in themselves great or small, God concerns himself with them; what affects them affects him; in all their afflictions he is afflicted. He who knows that God cares for him, need have no anxious cares about himself. This is a plain reference to <reference osisRef="Psa.55.22">Psa 55:22</reference> : Cast thy burden upon the Lord, and he will sustain thee. He will bear both thee and thy burden.
entries.0da9db98547cf6fd2dfae4aea836be9c6c401bb0: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen54726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54727" type="x-p"/> Be sober - Avoid drunkenness of your senses, and drunkenness in your souls; be not overcharged with the concerns of the world. <div eID="gen54727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54728" type="x-p"/> Be vigilant - Awake, and keep awake; be always watchful; never be off your guard; your enemies are alert, they are never off theirs. <div eID="gen54728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54729" type="x-p"/> Your adversary the devil - This is the reason why ye should be sober and vigilant; ye have an ever active, implacable, subtle enemy to contend with. He walketh about - he has access to you everywhere; he knows your feelings and your propensities, and informs himself of all your circumstances; only God can know more and do more than he, therefore your care must be cast upon God. <div eID="gen54729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54730" type="x-p"/> As a roaring lion - Satan tempts under three forms: <div eID="gen54730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54731" type="x-p"/> 1. The subtle serpent; to beguile our senses, pervert our judgment, and enchant our imagination. <div eID="gen54731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54732" type="x-p"/> 2. As an angel of light; to deceive us with false views of spiritual things, refinements in religion, and presumption on the providence and grace of God. <div eID="gen54732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54733" type="x-p"/> 3. As a roaring lion; to bear us down, and destroy us by violent opposition, persecution, and death. Thus he was acting towards the followers of God at Pontus, etc., who were now suffering a grievous persecution. <div eID="gen54733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54734" type="x-p"/> Walketh about - Traversing the earth; a plain reference to <reference osisRef="Job.2.2">Job 2:2</reference>, which see. <div eID="gen54734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54735" type="x-p"/> Seeking whom he may devour - Τινα καταπιῃ· Whom he may gulp down. It is not every one that he can swallow down: those who are sober and vigilant are proof against him, these he May Not swallow down; those who are drunken with the cares of this world, etc., and are unwatchful, these he May swallow down. There is a beauty in this verse, and a striking apposition between the first and last words, which I think have not been noticed: Be sober, νηψατε from νη, not, and πιειν to drink; do not drink, do not swallow down: and the word καταπιῃ, from κατα, down, and πιειν, to drink. If you swallow strong drink down, the devil will swallow you down. Hear this, ye drunkards, topers, tipplers, or by whatsoever name you are known in society, or among your fellow sinners. Strong drink is not only the way to the devil, but the devil's way into you; and Ye are such as the devil particularly May swallow down.
entries.74af7ff2ede98580ac87291dc6f58918e4f6cb38: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen54735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54736" type="x-p"/> Whom resist - Stand against him, αντιστητε. Though invulnerable, he is not unconquerable: the weakest follower of God can confound and overpower him, if he continue steadfast in the faith - believing on the Son of God, and walking uprightly before him. To a soul thus engaged he can do no damage. <div eID="gen54736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54737" type="x-p"/> The same afflictions are accomplished in your brethren - It is the lot of all the disciples of Christ to suffer persecution. The brotherhood, αδελφοτης, the Christian Church, everywhere is exposed to the assaults of men and devils; you are persecuted by the heathen among whom ye live, and from among whom ye are gathered into the fold of Christ: but even those who profess the same faith with you, and who are resident among the Jews, (for so I think εν κοσμῳ, in the world, is here to be understood), are also persecuted, both heathens and Jews being equally opposed to the pure and holy doctrines of the Gospel. Any man who has read the Greek Testament with any attention must have observed a vast number of places in which the word κοσμος, which we translate world, means the Jewish people and the Jewish state, and nothing else.
entries.e57d3bdeb134b94b99f9e281474055edae303046: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen54737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54738" type="x-p"/> But the God of all grace - The Fountain of infinite compassion, mercy, and goodness. Mohammed has conveyed this fine description of the Divine Being in the words with which he commences every surat or chapter of his Koran, two excepted; viz.; <div eID="gen54738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54739" type="x-p"/> Bismillahi arrahmani arraheemi. <div eID="gen54739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54740" type="x-p"/> Of which the best translation that can be given is that of the apostle, In the name of the God of all grace; the God who is the most merciful and the most compassionate, who is an exuberant Fountain of love and compassion to all his intelligent offspring. <div eID="gen54740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54741" type="x-p"/> Who hath called us - By the preaching of the Gospel. <div eID="gen54741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54742" type="x-p"/> Unto his eternal glory - To the infinite felicity of the heavenly state. <div eID="gen54742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54743" type="x-p"/> By Christ Jesus - Through the merit of his passion and death, by the influence of his Holy Spirit, by the precepts of his Gospel, and by the splendor of his own example. <div eID="gen54743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54744" type="x-p"/> After that ye have suffered a while - Ολιγον παθοντας· Having suffered a little time; that is, while ye are enduring these persecutions, God will cause all to work together for your good. <div eID="gen54744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54745" type="x-p"/> Make you perfect - Καταρτισει, στηριξει, σθενωσει, θεμελιωσει· All these words are read in the future tense by the best MSS. and versions. <div eID="gen54745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54746" type="x-p"/> He will make you perfect. - Καταρτισει· Put you in complete joint as the timbers of a building. <div eID="gen54746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54747" type="x-p"/> Stablish - Στηριξει· Make you firm in every part; adapt you strongly to each other, so that you may be mutual supports, the whole building being one in the Lord. <div eID="gen54747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54748" type="x-p"/> Strengthen - Σθενωσει· Cramp and bind every part, so that there shall be no danger of warping, splitting, or falling. <div eID="gen54748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen54749" type="x-p"/> Settle - Θεμελιωσει· Cause all to rest so evenly and firmly upon the best and surest foundation, that ye may grow together to a holy temple in the Lord: in a word, that ye may be complete in all the mind that was in Christ; supported in all your trials and difficulties; strengthened to resist and overcome all your enemies; and after all abide, firmly founded, in the truth of grace. All these phrases are architectural; and the apostle has again in view the fine image which he produced <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.5">1Pet 2:5</reference> (note).
